tone_statements.citation: Qu, Zhousuo & Cathryn Yang. 2019. Acoustic analysis of tone in Benna Hani: tone sandhi and neutralization in an atypical Tibeto-Burman language. In Sasha Calhoun, Paola Escudero, Marija Tabain & Paul Warren (eds.), Proceedings of the 19th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS 2019), Melbourne, 1967-1971. Canberra: ASSTA. Open PDF:https://www.internationalphoneticassociation.org/icphs-proceedings/ICPhS2019/papers/ICPhS_2016.pdf
tone_statements.quote: All Benna Hani tones have modal phonation, and duration is non-contrastive. All syllables, with a few exceptions, are specified for tone. Syllable structure is (C)V or syllabic nasal. The tone system has three contrastive tone categories, labelled as T1 (“High”), T2 (“Low”), and T3 (“Mid”). These categories transparently correspond to historical Proto-Ngwi (PN) tone categories [4]; modern reflexes of PN tone categories in Lüchun Hani [5] and Benna Hani are compared in Table 1. There are two major points of divergence with Lüchun Hani: 1) Benna Hani has lost contrastive tense phonation, leading to a merger of Proto-Ngwi *H with T3 and *L with T2, respectively;
tone_statements.locator: p. 1967, section 1 Introduction (with Table 1 'Proto-Ngwi, Lüchun and Benna Hani tone')
tone_statements.summary: Benna Hani: 3 tones (T1 H, T2 L, T3 M), modal phonation only, syllable TBU, heavy sandhi with T1/T3 neutralization in non-final position; Lüchun (standard) Hani: 55, 31, 33 plus tense-voice 33 and 31.

sources.citation: Hansson, Inga-Lill. 1982. A phonological comparison of Akha and Hani. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 7(1): 63-115.
sources.note: Silent. Segmental and tonal comparison of Lüchun Hani (1959 Hani-Chinese wordlist + 1981 tape) with Akha; describes 3 tones (High -l, Mid -zero, Low -q) plus laryngealized Mid -v / Low -vq. No occurrence of 'stress', 'accent' or 'prominence' in the 53 scanned pages.

sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A. 2002. The Central and Southern Loloish languages of Vietnam. Proceedings of BLS 28, Special Session on Tibeto-Burman and Southeast Asian Linguistics: 1-13. DOI 10.3765/bls.v28i2.1042
sources.note: Section 5 'Hani (Hahni)' (pp. 8-11) gives Vietnam Hani (Muong Te) tones 55/31/33 plus two glottally constricted syllable shapes [31ʔ] [33ʔ], initials, and comparisons with Lüchun Hani and Akha; nothing on stress. sources.note: Instrumental (aerodynamic and acoustic) study of the 'tense' vs 'lax' syllable contrast in Hani alongside Jingpho, Yi and Wa: shows the contrast is primarily one of phonation type - lax vowels have greater oral airflow relative to subglottal pressure and a stronger fundamental relative to the second harmonic (H1-H2) than tense vowels, with vowel quality, duration and adjacent-consonant effects involved only inconsistently. For Hani this is the register dimension that combines with the three pitch tones (55/33/31, tense register absent with 55 per Wheatley 1982), i.e. the phonetic basis of the…

sources.note: Per Wheatley 1982:3 it is 'a discussion on the incidence of a tense versus lax vowel quality distinction' in Lüchun Hani with tonally transcribed forms; Hansson 1982 and Bradley 1977 use its data for tone correspondences (Bradley cites from it a dialect with constricted 55/33 vs plain 33/21 tones). Likely the primary statement of how the tense/lax register co-occurs with the Hani tones (tense syllables only in the 33 and 31 tones per the later summaries), i.e. the phonation-tone interaction of standard Hani.
